title: Architecture Trade-offs
subtitle: Decision frameworks, reversible versus one-way doors, ADRs, and managing binding constraints.
keyTakeaways: There is no universally superior architecture, only trade-offs selected against specific binding constraints (latency, consistency, cost, team structure, and compliance).

Separate Type 1 decisions (one-way doors with severe switching costs: primary sharding keys, database engines, public API contracts) from Type 2 decisions (two-way doors: cache TTLs, internal library choices).

Capture architectural decisions in written Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) that explicitly state rejected alternatives, quantitative assumptions, and the scale triggers that will invalidate the decision.

sections.heading: Evaluating Constraints and Navigating One-Way Doors
sections.body: Junior engineers look for the "best" tool; senior engineers identify the binding constraint and determine what they are willing to sacrifice. Every architectural decision is an exercise in constraint optimization, where optimizing for one axis (like sub-millisecond read latency) degrades another (like transactional consistency or infrastructure spend).
bullets: Identifying the binding constraint: A real-time stock trading engine is bound by tail latency and deterministic execution; a medical records platform is bound by auditability and regulatory compliance; an early-stage startup is bound by developer iteration velocity. Designing without identifying your primary constraint leads to over-engineering the wrong attributes.

One-way vs two-way doors: Jeff Bezos popularized categorizing decisions into irreversible Type 1 (one-way doors) and reversible Type 2 (two-way doors). Choosing your primary database partitioning key or an asynchronous event-sourced ledger is a Type 1 decision that takes quarters to undo. Choosing an HTTP client library or a cache eviction TTL is a Type 2 decision that can be rolled back in an afternoon.

The Conway's Law constraint: Systems mirror the communication structures of the organizations that build them. Splitting a service into ten fine-grained microservices when you have a four-person engineering team creates operational friction and communication overhead that outweighs any technical benefit.

codeSnippet.title: Staff-Grade Architecture Decision Record (ADR) Template
codeSnippet.code:
# ADR-042: Event-Sourced Ledger vs ACID Relational State for Wallet Balances
- Status: Accepted (2026-09-30)
- Context: Need 15,000 TPS peak wallet transfers, strict auditability, < 50ms p99.

## Considered Options
1. Single-Region Partitioned PostgreSQL (Double-Entry Ledger Table + Row Locks)
2. Kafka + Custom In-Memory Event-Sourced State Machine
3. CockroachDB Multi-Region Distributed SQL

## Decision & Trade-Off Rationale
- Chosen: Option 1 (Hash-Partitioned PostgreSQL by account_id across 16 shards).
- Why Rejected #2: Rebuilding in-memory snapshots and handling split-brain adds
  high operational risk for a 6-engineer team.
- Why Rejected #3: Cross-region Raft consensus adds 45ms WAN latency, breaching p99.
- Re-Evaluation Trigger: Revisit when peak exceeds 80,000 TPS or multi-region
  active-active regulatory mandate is introduced.

sections.heading: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as Living Contracts
sections.body: Undocumented architecture decisions lead to "chesterton's fence" paralysis: two years later, new engineers see an awkward piece of design and cannot tell whether it is an intentional workaround for an esoteric edge case or outdated technical debt.
bullets: Documenting rejected alternatives: The most valuable part of an ADR is not the chosen solution, but the explicit list of alternatives considered and rejected, along with the concrete reasons why they were disqualified.

Defining invalidation triggers: Every ADR should include explicit scale or domain triggers that will render the decision obsolete (e.g., "This single-node PostgreSQL primary handles our current 2,000 QPS; if write volume exceeds 12,000 QPS or table size passes 4 TB, we will evaluate horizontal sharding").

Preventing architectural drift: Make ADR reviews part of the standard design review process. When engineers understand the historical constraints behind legacy components, they make informed refactoring decisions instead of repeating old mistakes.

tradeOffs.option: Fast Decision Velocity (Biased Toward Type 2 Experimentation)
tradeOffs.pros: Enables rapid product iteration; discovers real user requirements quickly through live production feedback.
tradeOffs.cons: Can inadvertently make hasty Type 1 commitments (like picking an immature database) that accumulate technical debt.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Seed-stage features, internal experimental tools, and consumer application frontends.

tradeOffs.option: Rigorous Architecture Review Process (ADR Gates for Type 1)
tradeOffs.pros: Prevents expensive, multi-quarter migrations caused by short-sighted data model and storage choices.
tradeOffs.cons: Slows initial project kickoff; risks analysis paralysis if applied uniformly to low-stakes implementation details.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core ledger systems, identity and access control frameworks, and foundational data storage engines.

interviewTip: Demonstrate staff-level seniority by framing architectural choices in terms of one-way vs two-way doors. When choosing a database or sharding key, explain why it is a one-way door that demands careful constraint analysis, whereas choosing an in-memory caching layer is a reversible two-way door.
